h1: Cask finishing times and how to judge them
title: Judging Cask Finishing Times | Craft Beer School
desc: How long to finish whisky in a second cask and how to judge readiness with sampling, controls and simple scoring in hot conditions.
teaser: There is no right finishing time. There is only the day the whisky tastes right. You find it by sampling.
standfirst: A cask finish can last weeks or years. The time depends on the cask, the climate and the whisky. What makes a finish work is a sampling routine that catches the moment the finish has done enough and not more.
sections: A finish adds a layer, not a new whisky

Finishing means moving a mature whisky into a second cask, often one that held wine, sherry, port or rum, for a shorter final period. The goal is a layer of new flavour on top of the original character. Our guide to cask finishing in whisky covers the basics.

The risk on one side is a finish too short to notice. On the other side it takes over. The whisky then tastes of the second cask and little else. Time is how you steer between them.

Several things set how fast a finish works:

  • Cask activity. A freshly emptied, wet cask works far faster than a dry or tired one.
  • Cask size. A 225 litre barrique works faster than a 500 litre butt.
  • Temperature. Warm warehouses speed extraction. Indian heat can turn a Scottish year into a few months.
  • Strength. Spirit strength changes which compounds come out of the wood.
  • Base whisky. A delicate whisky shows the finish sooner than a heavy one.

In cool climates, finishes of a few months to two years are common. In India, start from the assumption that things will move much faster.
Set up a sampling plan before you fill

Decide the sampling schedule on day one. A sensible plan for an active cask in Indian conditions:

  1. Retain a control sample of the base whisky before it goes into the finishing cask.
  2. Sample at two to four weeks.
  3. Then every two to four weeks until the finish is close, then weekly.
  4. Keep every sample in a sealed, labelled bottle so you can line them up.

The floor detail we insist on: draw each sample from the same depth with the same valinch, after rolling or rocking the cask gently if it has been still for a while. Spirit near the bung can differ from the middle. A misleading sample leads to a wrong call.
Judge against the control, not memory

Taste the finishing sample beside the control at around 20% ABV, diluted with clean water. Your memory of the base whisky drifts. The control does not.

Score a few things each time on a simple 1 to 5 scale: base whisky character, finish character, tannin and dryness, any faults. Plot them. A healthy finish shows finish character rising while the base stays recognisable. When the finish score climbs past the base score, or tannin rises sharply, you are close to the end or past it. Our guide to maturation and casks explains where tannin comes from.
Signs a finish has gone too far

Watch for these:

  • Drying, bitter tannin that coats the mouth.
  • A pink or purple tint from a red wine cask.
  • Sulphur notes growing stronger with each sample.
  • The base whisky's character fading from the nose.

If you overshoot, blending is often the rescue. A small share of over-finished whisky mixed back into unfinished stock can give a balanced result. That is why many distillers finish only part of a batch and blend.

A worked example: if 20% of a vatting has been finished hard in an active red wine barrique and the remaining 80% is unfinished, the blend can carry a clear wine note with far less of the tannin of the finished portion alone. Bench test a few ratios in millilitres before you vat, because the right share depends on how far the finish went.

Finishing affects more than flavour. Regauge before and after so you know the litres of pure alcohol going in and coming out. Short finishes in active, wet casks can lose a surprising amount of spirit to wood soakage alone. Strength can shift too, especially if wine or rum was left in the cask.

Those numbers feed the cost of the finished product. Our guide to how whisky is made shows where finishing sits in the full cost chain.

Good finishing comes from a repeatable method more than a gifted palate: a control, a schedule, a scoring sheet and records. With that, a team can make the call consistently. The next finish starts with real data. Learning to set up and read that method is part of what a distilling course gives you.

Your first step: before your next finish goes into cask, bottle a control sample and print a scoring sheet with dates already filled in for the first three months.
faqs: How long should a whisky cask finish last?
There is no fixed time. Cool climate finishes often run from months to two years. In hot Indian warehouses an active cask may need only weeks.
How do I know when a finish is ready?
Sample regularly against a retained control of the base whisky and stop when the finish character sits alongside the base rather than covering it.
What happens if a whisky is over-finished?
It can turn tannic and bitter, lose its original character or take on too much colour. Blending it with unfinished stock can often rescue it.
Memory of a whisky drifts over months. A sealed control lets you compare every finishing sample with what the whisky was before.
